substance: Acquisition Network started at zero: no GTM system, no lead flow, no sales process. A strong product with no engine behind it. Revenue happened in spurts and depended entirely on the founder's personal network. Result: $0 to $2.9M generated, in about two years, and the founder stopped being the funnel himself. Ryan also built the company's own application/product, so the engagement covered both the product and the system that sold it.

title: Case study: Malik Consolidated
substance: Malik Consolidated had limited GTM infrastructure: some sales process in place, but no funnel strategy, no CRM workflow, no campaign execution layer, no lead-to-close conversion system. Ryan engaged as Growth Marketing Consultant. Started somewhere harder than zero: a CRM, funnels, and a pipeline that had never talked to each other, built by different hands at different times. The seams between the pieces were exactly where revenue leaked. Built the connective tissue: one cohesive funnel instead of several, CRM automations at every stage (no manual handoffs), ads/pages/nurture on one calendar, every drop-off made visible and fixed one leak at a time. The result was not more leads, it was fewer dropped ones; conversion rose at every step because every step finally handed off cleanly. Total generated: $1.6M, about a two-year engagement.

title: Case study: Big Little Gyms
substance: Big Little Gyms was a 15-client coaching business at the start of a major demand spike (the pandemic). Established offer, but acquisition, fulfillment, and client-experience systems were all manual and founder-dependent. Ryan engaged as Growth Operations Lead. The problem was never getting attention; demand exploded overnight. The problem was not breaking under the weight of it. Built acquisition (capture, qualify, route), fulfillment (onboarding automation, group-coaching infrastructure), and client-experience systems (check-ins, community, retention loops) all at once, because the business could not afford to sequence them. Daily standups and weekly KPI review through the spike; four coaches recruited while the client count multiplied. Result: 15 to 189 clients in 11 months, 12x growth, $989K total revenue, no quality crash, no retention crater.

title: Case study: MachineryMaps
substance: MachineryMaps (a crane and heavy-equipment rental client) had a site that could only ask a visitor to call. Ryan's team is building software that transacts instead: listings with real availability, quote capture that lands in the CRM instead of a voicemail, insurance upload inside the order flow, e-signature on the rental agreement. Key rule: the deposit is authorized on the card, not captured, until the owner approves the order, enforced at every entry point, so a bad booking never leaves the yard and a customer is never charged for one the owner has not seen. Architecture decision: the storefront and a future multi-vendor marketplace share one codebase, so nothing gets built twice; the client launches as the first vendor. This is in-build (not yet generating disclosed revenue) and led primarily by Ryan's developer.

title: VSL v2.29 doctrine (AI implementation)
substance: Core doctrine from the approved VSL: AI is not going to replace a business; a competitor whose team uses AI better will, a little more every month, and it compounds until one day you cannot compete. Most owners have only seen the ChatGPT version of AI (one person using it like a toy, nothing wired into the actual work, nothing measured). Five areas AI pays off: marketing (audits every ad you and competitors have run, hyper-targeted creative, funnels built in minutes), sales (CRM updates itself, call tracking, follow-up within minutes), fulfillment (onboarding runs itself, first-draft reports), operations (dashboards and trackers build themselves), and the foundation, God Mode: an AI coworker trained on the whole business (SOPs, pipeline, calls, ads, KPIs) that already knows the answer to 'which campaign made money last month' and has drafted the fix. The order that works: build the coworker first, use it to find the ONE constraint capping the business, then build systems aimed only at that constraint; installing AI where it's easy instead of where the constraint is (automating a newsletter while leads sit six hours) is the most common mistake. Most ad accounts we open have broken attribution and no real KPI dashboard (say 'most', not a specific percentage, since the harder stat could not be sourced). Proof stack (safe, from the approved script): Smart Sellers Academy $1.5M in about eighteen months; Acquisition Network from an idea to $2.9M in about two years; All Done Consulting from a small monthly base to $4.6M; this year Ryan and his business partner launched an AI software company with no developers, in under three months. Koolaid line: the same AI-assisted systems used for clients are run on Ryan's own marketing first.
canonicalNumbers: $1.5M, $2.9M, $4.6M as in the other sources. Say 'most' not '98%' for the attribution stat.
angleIdeas: AI won't replace your business

title: Cold outreach: what changed after testing
substance: Lessons from building and testing a cold-outreach system. The word 'AI' was removed from the first line of every outbound message, because every prospect's inbox already has an AI pitch in it and it reads as noise before the second sentence. It was replaced with one true, specific, verifiable observation about the prospect's own funnel (their booking page fires a lead event on page load instead of on a completed booking; their ad has run for weeks with no tracking tag so the CRM can't attribute a booked call to an ad). The rule that came with it: every finding is checked against a screenshot or a timestamp before it goes out, because a wrong finding is not just embarrassing, it damages trust. A separate earlier stat, 'about $1,200 lost per missed call', turned out to be a vendor's repeated math built on a $4,500 job at a certain margin; the honest, defensible version is to describe a concrete example job and its real numbers rather than repeat an unverified industry-wide average. Also corrected: an earlier internal estimate of 'one meeting per 25 dials' was unverified; the realistic planning number for cold calling is closer to one meeting per 150 dials.
canonicalNumbers: N/A - describes methodology corrections, not dollar totals

title: Expert Health product-label AI rule
substance: Standard operating rule for Expert Health's product photography pipeline: the AI image model is never allowed to draw the logo, the label text, or the product name directly, because a health brand runs on trust and a render that gives away its own artificiality (a slightly wrong wordmark, inconsistent shape) damages that trust. Instead the bottle photo is generated blank-label, and the real branding (logo, name, layout) is composited on top in code from one master template, recolored per product line, so every bottle in the catalog shares the same size, position, and layout, and only the color and name change. The general lesson: let the AI do the part it is good at (photorealistic rendering) and hard-code the part where a mistake costs trust (exact brand text).

title: Voice sample: the tactics graveyard
substance: STRUCTURE ONLY, no vendor names. A list of things a stuck founder has usually already tried: a VA (still the bottleneck because every decision needed him), a course (knew the content by module three, nothing installed), an ads agency (ninety days of 'we're optimizing' and a deck of vanity metrics, then blame the offer when calls don't book), a sales coach (the right script, still closing every call himself), a fractional CMO or a mastermind (showed up to the meeting, moved nothing). title: Voice sample: order-takers
substance: STRUCTURE ONLY. Contrarian claim: a sales team should be order-takers. Right now most closers do three jobs at once: educating the lead, convincing the lead, and closing the lead, which is why the best rep is exhausted. In the better version, the ad already called out exactly who it's for, the funnel already made the case, qualification already filtered for fit, so the person on the call already believes; that's a pre-sold appointment. What's left for sales is confirming fit, handling real questions, and taking the order, not because the closers got lazy, but because the system in front of them got competent.
